title: PKM2 + apoptotic vesicle-mediated systemic senolytics ameliorate chronic periodontitis

sections.abstract: Chronic periodontitis (CP) is one of the most prevalent local inflammatory disorders and is associated with various systemic diseases. However, the relationship between local CP pathogenesis and systemic metabolic responses is not fully elucidated. In this study, we show that CP causes systemic inflammation, leading to apoptotic resistance and senescent cell accumulation, which are crucial for maintaining local inflammation in a CP mouse model. Eliminating senescent cells through systemic senolytic therapy ameliorate local CP pathological changes. Proteomic analysis reveals that CP patient plasma extracellular vesicles show upregulation of immune response-related proteins and downregulation of metabolic and apoptosis-related proteins, among which pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2) was significantly reduced. Moreover, CP mice show reduced circulating apoptotic vesicles (apoVs), particularly those carrying PKM2. Systemic administration of PKM2 + mesenchymal stem cell-derived apoVs (MSC-apoVs) effectively rescues apoptotic resistance, eliminates senescent cells, and mitigates CP phenotypes. Mechanistically, we show that chronic inflammation reduces the level of nuclear PKM2 to promote apoptotic resistance. Systemic infusion of PKM2 + MSC-apoVs facilitates the nuclear translocation of PKM2 to alleviate apoptotic resistance and eliminate senescent cells. Our findings suggest that elimination of senescent cells as a new strategy for CP treatment. In addition, we propose the concept that systemic metabolism may determine the maintenance of local inflammation pathogenesis in CP.
sections.introduction:
Persistent chronic inflammation has significant impacts on the development and progression of chronic diseases including diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, cardiovascular disease, neurodegenerative conditions, and cancer [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ]. Accumulating experimental evidence indicates that chronic inflammation frequently coexists with apoptotic resistance. The relationship between apoptotic resistance and chronic inflammation is complex and multifaceted. Chronic inflammation can stimulate the elevation of anti-apoptotic proteins, alter mitochondrial function, suppress caspase activation, and promote cellular senescence, thereby contributing to the development of apoptotic resistance [ 6 ]. However, the precise mechanisms of chronic inflammation that leads to apoptotic resistance remain unclear.

Periodontitis is a widespread inflammatory disease of the tooth-supporting soft and bony tissues, leading to low-grade systemic inflammation [ 7 ]. Chronic periodontitis (CP) can lead to the release of systemic inflammatory factors, such as IL-17, IL-1β, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and C-reactive protein (CRP) [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. Elevated levels of these molecules are associated with an increased risk of developing various chronic diseases, further highlighting the connection between chronic periodontitis and systemic diseases. Prolonged exposure to these inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-1β, has been shown to impair normal apoptotic processes and contribute to apoptotic resistance [ 11 , 12 ]. Apoptotic resistance is a hallmark of cellular senescence, enabling damaged or dysfunctional cells to evade clearance and persist within tissues [ 13 ]. These senescent cells adopt a pro-inflammatory phenotype known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), thereby perpetuating inflammation and tissue dysfunction. Given that chronic systemic inflammation can impair apoptotic processes, we hypothesize that apoptotic resistance may be a critical mechanism linking CP to its systemic pathological effects.

Apoptotic cell-derived vesicles (ApoVs) carry various cellular components, such as DNA, RNA, proteins, and lipids [ 14 ]. These vesicles contribute to tissue homeostatic maintenance and metabolic regulation. Our previous studies have demonstrated that mesenchymal stem cell-derived apoVs (MSC-apoVs) can treat a variety of diseases including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), arthritis, osteopenia, multiple myeloma, sepsis, and type 2 diabetes [ [15] , [16] , [17] , [18] , [19] , [20] ]. These findings suggest that a reduction of apoVs due to apoptotic resistance may be involved in the development of chronic inflammatory disease.

Pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2) is a critical regulator of inflammation and apoptosis. Under immune stimulation, such as exposure to LPS, PKM2 can translocate to the nucleus, where it interacts with transcription factors like HIF-1α and STAT3 to activate the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-1β and TNF-α [ 21 , 22 ]. PKM2 is also highly expressed in M1-type macrophages, where it plays a vital role in maintaining their pro-inflammatory phenotype and supports the metabolic reprogramming necessary for inflammatory responses by regulating aerobic glycolysis [ 23 , 24 ].

Beyond its classical role as a key glycolysis enzyme, PKM2 modulates apoptosis through diverse mechanisms. Within the nucleus, it can interact with transcription factors STAT3, HIF-1α, and β-catenin to promote the transcription of anti-apoptotic and proliferation-associated genes [ [25] , [26] , [27] ]. Also, several studies have shown that PKM2 can facilitate apoptosis, various apoptotic stimuli promote its nuclear translocation, triggering cell death through pathways that are independent of caspase activation [ 28 ]. Moreover, inhibition of PKM2 expression can enhance its nuclear localization, leading to cell cycle arrest and apoptosis [ 29 ]. PKM2 aggregation has been detected in senescent cells and tissues, and this phenomenon is thought to contribute to the progression of cellular senescent state [ 30 ]. Collectively, these findings suggest that the nuclear translocation and aggregation of PKM2 may play pivotal roles in regulating inflammation-associated cellular senescence and apoptosis resistance. Additionally, emerging evidence indicates that PKM2 may exert its biological effects via exosome-mediated transfer, contributing to intercellular communication in both physiological and pathological contexts [ 31 ]. Therefore, investigating changes in vesicle-associated PKM2 under chronic inflammatory conditions such as periodontitis may offer new insights into disease pathogenesis and uncover potential therapeutic targets.

Currently, CP treatment is primarily focused on removing local irritants and promoting local bone regeneration. However, chronic inflammation caused by periodontitis can lead to systemic pathological changes, such as long-lasting myeloid differentiation bias of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) and the induction of clonal hematopoiesis in the bone marrow [ 32 , 33 ]. Therefore, systemic treatment strategies may offer a promising new approach for achieving more comprehensive management of CP. In this study, we show that apoptotic metabolites carried by MSC-apoVs are associated with apoptotic balance. Furthermore, MSC-apoVs rescue apoptotic resistance not only by directly transporting PKM2 into the nuclei of senescent cells, but also by promoting Ser37 phosphorylation of endogenous PKM2 to facilitate its nuclear import.
sections.methods:
Wild-type C57BL/6 mice (male, 4 weeks old), PKM2 +/− mice (male, 4 weeks old) and PKM2-eGFP mice (male, 4 weeks old) were obtained from Guangdong GemPharmatech Co., Ltd. and used for mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) isolation. Wild-type C57BL/6 mice (male, 10 weeks old), also sourced from Guangdong GemPharmatech Co., Ltd., were used to establish the ligature-induced periodontitis model. All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU-IACUC-202300031).

Male C57BL/6 mice at aged 4–6 weeks are commonly used to isolate MSCs due to their high cellular activity and ease of in vitro expansion [ 34 ]. Therefore, we selected 4-week-old male mice for MSC isolation. For the periodontitis model, we used silk threads soaked with porphyromonas gingivalis to induce periodontitis. The most studies used 8–10-week-old mice to generate periodontitis model [ 35 , 36 ]. Thus, we used 10-week-old mice to establish periodontitis model.

All antibodies, chemicals, and other reagents used in this study were listed in Supplementary Table 1 .

The ligature-induced periodontitis model was established as previously described [ 35 , 36 ]. Briefly, 10-week-old wild-type C57BL/6 mice were anesthetized, and P. gingivalis -soaked 5–0 silk ligatures were tied around the maxillary second molars (bilaterally). Ligatures remained in place for 3, 6, 15, 30, or 60 days, as indicated in the figure legends, with all animals euthanized simultaneously.

To establish the short-term periodontitis model, mice underwent ligature placement for 15 days to induce periodontitis, followed by ligature removal and a 30-day recovery period without further intervention. For the long-term periodontitis model, ligatures were placed for 60 days, followed by a 30-day recovery period. This design enabled us to evaluate the natural healing capacity and tissue regeneration following transient versus prolonged inflammatory insults.

For therapeutic intervention, ligatures were removed after 60 days, followed by a four-week treatment regimen. Mice were administered dasatinib (5 mg/kg body weight) and quercetin (50 mg/kg body weight), dissolved in 10 % polyethylene glycol 4000, once weekly [ 37 ]. Control mice were given a vehicle solution (10 % polyethylene glycol 4000). For MSC and MSC-apoV treatments, mice received intravenous tail vein injections of either adipose-derived MSCs (1 × 10 6 ) or adipose MSC-derived apoptotic vesicles (MSC-apoVs; 100 μL, 4 × 10 9 ) once weekly for four weeks [ 16 , 38 ]. Control mice were given a vehicle solution (PBS).

After euthanizing mice at 4 weeks of age, bone marrow cells were flushed out of the bone marrow of mice femurs with 5 % fetal bovine serum (FBS) in PBS. Single-cell suspension was obtained by passing through a 70 μm cell strainer (BD Biosciences, USA). Cells were incubated for 48 h at 37 °C in 5 % CO 2 . The non-adherent cells were washed out with PBS, and mouse bone marrow MSCs (BMMSCs) were cultured for 10 days with alpha minimum essential medium supplemented with 20 % FBS, 2 mM L-glutamine, 50 mM 2-mercaptoethanol, 100 U/ml penicillin and 100 mg ml −1 streptomycin. Cells were used from passage 3 to 5 for further experiments.

Adipose-derived MSCs were selected because adipose tissue is readily accessible and yields a high abundance of MSCs [ 39 ]. Additionally, our preliminary data indicate that apoVs from MSCs of different sources show no significant differences in apoV protein content, further supporting the choice of fat-derived MSC-apoVs for treating chronic periodontitis (CP) [ 40 ]. After euthanizing the mice at 4 weeks of age, subcutaneous and visceral adipose tissues were isolated. The tissues were minced with scissors, then subjected to enzymatic digestion with 2 mg ml −1 collagenase type 1 (Worthington Biochemical, USA) and 4 mg ml −1 dispase II (Roche Diagnostics, Switzerland) for 1 h at 37 °C. The digestion was neutralized with medium supplemented with 15 % FBS. The mixture was centrifuged at 500 g for 5 min at 4 °C to pellet cells. The supernatant was discarded, and the cell pellet was resuspended, filtered through a 70 μm cell strainer, and seeded into culture dishes. MSCs were cultured at 37 °C in 5 % CO 2 in α-MEM supplemented with 15 % FBS, 2 mM L-glutamine, 50 μM 2-mercaptoethanol, 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 μg/mL streptomycin. Cells were passaged to generations 2–3 for subsequent MSC-apoVs induction. MSCs were then incubated with staurosporine (STS) (250 nM) to induce apoptosis. The supernatant was collected and subjected to sequential centrifugation (800 g for 10 min, 2000 g for 10 min, and 16000 g for 30 min) to separate MSC-apoVs. MSC-apoVs were washed twice with filtered PBS before use.

Human plasma samples were obtained from 6 periodontitis patients and 6 healthy volunteers from Guanghua School of Stomatology, Sun Yat-sen University. Periodontitis was diagnosed according to the 2018 new classification and definition of periodontitis, as well as the definition of healthy control. Human sample collection was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of the Hospital of Stomatology, Sun Yat-sen University (KQEC-2023-31-02). All participants in this study signed an informed consent form prior to sample collection.

Mouse plasma samples were collected from whole blood obtained via retro-orbital arterial bleeding under anesthesia.

For circulating vesicle isolation, plasma from human or mouse was subjected to sequential centrifugation at 4 °C: 800 g for 10 min to remove cells, then 2000 g for 10 min to remove debris. Circulating vesicle precipitation was obtained by centrifuging the supernatant at 16000 g for 30 min and 120,000 g for 2 h.

Extracellular vesicles from human plasma were obtained as described above and then protein lysates were prepared and subjected to nano-LC-MS/MS analysis. For proteomic analysis, Q-Exactive HF (Thermo Fisher Scientific, San Jose, CA) was used to acquire mass spectrometry (MS) data in data independent acquisition (DIA) mode and data dependent acquisition (DDA) mode. The mixed samples went through mass spectrometry data collection in DDA mode. The raw data from DDA were processed and analyzed by MaxQuant (version 1.5.3.30) with the Andromeda search engine. To build the library, each sample went through mass spectrometry data collection in DIA mode, and quantification of peptides and proteins was performed using Spectronaut™ and MSstats software packages. The quality of the data was evaluated based on the intra-group coefficient of variation (CV), principal component analysis (PCA), and quantitative correlation of samples. Proteins were identified by comparing against the Uniprot database with a false discovery rate (FDR) set at 0.01 for both peptides and proteins. Proteins that were significantly upregulated in apoVs (Fold change >2 and adjusted p-value <0.05) were included for further functional analysis based on Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) and Gene Ontology (GO) databases.

Proteomic data from apoVs and exosomes derived from human bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), obtained from previously generated datasets, were analyzed to compare PKM expression [ 40 ]. Protein identification and quantification were performed using MaxQuant, with proteins matched against the Uniprot database (FDR <0.01). PKM expression was found to be significantly higher in apoVs than exosomes (Fold change >2, adjusted p-value <0.05).

To abrogate PKM2 expression in adipose-derived MSC-apoVs, the MSCs (60–70 % confluent) were transfected with siRNA-negative control (si-NC) or siRNA-PKM2 (si-PKM2) (RIBOBIO, China) using the Lipofectamine™ RNAiMAX Transfection Reagent (Invitrogen, USA) and Opti-MEM Medium (Gibco, USA), following the manufacturer's directions. Transfection efficiency was evaluated at 48 h post-transfection via Western blotting. Adipose-derived MSCs transfected with siRNA (120 nM) for 72 h were used for apoV isolation.

Peripheral blood was collected from mice into EDTA anticoagulant tubes and diluted 1:1 with sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). The diluted blood was carefully layered onto lymphocyte separation medium (Solarbio, China) and centrifuged at 400 g for 30 min at room temperature with the brake off. The middle whitish layer (mononuclear cells) was aspirated, washed twice with PBS by centrifugation at 300 g for 10 min at 4 °C, and resuspended in RPMI 1640 medium (Gibco, USA) supplemented with 10 % FBS for downstream analysis.

Spleens and cervical lymph nodes were excised from euthanized mice and placed in ice-cold PBS. Tissues were mechanically dissociated by grinding through a 70 μm cell strainer in RPMI 1640 medium with 10 % FBS. The cell suspensions were centrifuged at 300 g for 10 min at 4 °C to pellet cells. For spleen samples, red blood cells were lysed with ACK lysis buffer (Thermo Fisher, USA) for 3 min at room temperature, followed by neutralization with PBS and centrifugation. Cell pellets from both spleen and cervical lymph nodes were resuspended in RPMI 1640 with 10 % FBS for further analysis.

Cells from peripheral blood, spleen, and cervical lymph nodes were stained for surface markers with antibodies including: APC anti-mouse CD4 (BioLegend, USA), FITC anti-mouse CD25 (BioLegend, USA), Pacific Blue anti-mouse CD8 (BioLegend, USA). For intracellular staining, cells were fixed and permeabilized using the Foxp3/Transcription Factor Staining Buffer Set (Thermo Fisher Scientific, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer's instructions, followed by staining with PE anti-mouse Foxp3 (BioLegend, USA) for Treg cells, PE anti-mouse IL-17 (BioLegend, USA) for Th17 cells. Prior to Th17 staining, cells were stimulated with 50 ng/mL PMA (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) and 1 μg/mL ionomycin (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) in the presence of GolgiStop (BD Biosciences, USA) for 4–6 h at 37 °C in 5 % CO 2 .

For apoptosis assays, cells were stained with FITC anti-Annexin V (BD Biosciences, USA) and PE-Cy7-conjugated anti-7AAD (BD Biosciences, USA) for 15 min at room temperature in the dark, according to the manufacturer's protocol. Stained cells were analyzed using a NovoCyte flow cytometer (Agilent Technologies, USA). Data were processed with NovoExpress software (Agilent Technologies, USA).

We measured the relative abundance of immune cell populations (e.g., Th17, Treg, CD4 + , CD8 + ) across conditions over time using flow cytometry as described above. Due to varying cell counts across tissues, we normalized the data for the heatmaps. For each cell type, non-normalized data were used to calculate ratios relative to the control, then scaled from 0 (“min,” lowest ratio) to 1 (“max,” highest ratio) across all conditions and time points. This enabled comparison of relative changes, visualized with colors from blue (low) to red (high).

Plasma concentrations of IL-17, IL-1β, TNF-α, TNF-β, IFN-γ, and IL-16 were measured using murine Quantikine ELISA kits (MAISHA, China) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, serum samples were diluted as recommended, added to pre-coated 96-well plates, and incubated with detection antibodies and streptavidin-HRP conjugate. After washing, TMB substrate was added, and absorbance was measured at 450 nm (corrected at 540 nm) using a microplate reader (BioTek Synergy H1). Concentrations were calculated from standard curves.

Peripheral blood samples were collected in EDTA anticoagulant tubes and processed within 2 h of collection to ensure accuracy. CBC analysis was performed using an automated hematology analyzer (SINNOWA, China). The following parameters were measured: white blood cell count (WBC), lymphocyte count, monocyte count, and granulocyte count, along with the percentage of each type of white blood cell in its own group was calculated. It is important to note that the percentages of lymphocytes, monocytes, and granulocytes presented in the CBC data were reported independently by the hematology analyzer based on different gating strategies. Slight overlaps in classification or rounding errors during automated analysis may result in a cumulative percentage exceeding 100 %, which is a common limitation in some hematological instruments.

Maxillary jaws were dissected from euthanized mice, fixed in 4 % paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 24 h, and analyzed using a Venus Micro CT scanner (PINGSENG Healthcare, China) with the scan parameters of tube voltage 90 kV, tube current 70 μA, and voxel size 13 μm. Three-dimensional reconstructions were generated and analyzed using Avatar software (PINGSENG Healthcare, China). Alveolar bone loss was quantified in the palatal region by measuring the cementoenamel junction to alveolar bone crest (CEJ-ABC) area, calculated as the area between the CEJ and ABC contours in sagittal sections of the maxillary second molar.

Jaws, femurs, livers, spleens, and kidneys of mice were harvested and fixed in 4 % PFA at 4 °C for 24 h. Jaws and femurs were decalcified in 10 % EDTA (pH 7.0) for 3 weeks at room temperature with weekly solution changes. Tissues were then dehydrated, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned. Sections were deparaffinized and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (HE) following standard protocols. Images were acquired using an optical microscope (Zeiss, Germany) with 10x objective for jaws and 20x for other tissues.

For immunofluorescence, fresh tissues were dissected, embedded in optimal cutting temperature (OCT) compound, and sectioned. Sections were fixed in ice-cold 4 % PFA for 10 min, washed with PBS, and subjected to antigen retrieval in citrate buffer (10 mM, pH 6.0) at 95 °C for 20 min. After cooling, sections were blocked with 5 % bovine serum albumin (BSA) in PBS for 1 h at room temperature, then incubated overnight at 4 °C with anti-p16 antibody (1:100). Sections were washed with PBS and incubated with secondary antibody (1:100) for 1 h at room temperature in the dark. Slides were imaged using LSM980 (Zeiss, Germany) with a 63x objective. To quantify the p16 positive rate, images were analyzed using ImageJ. A signal intensity threshold was set to identify positive staining, distinguishing it from background. The positive cells were calculated as a percentage of the total cell count in each field of view. For each sample, 4 fields of view were analyzed, and the average positive rate was reported.

To identify osteoclasts within the jaw tissue, TRAP staining was performed using a TRAP staining kit (Wako, Japan). The tissue sections were incubated with the TRAP staining solution, prepared according to the manufacturer's instructions, at 37 °C for 60 min. The staining solution consisted of an acetate buffer (pH 5.0) containing 50 mM sodium tartrate, 0.1 mg mL −1 naphthol AS-BI phosphate as the substrate, and Fast Red TR salt as the chromogen. Images were acquired using an optical microscope (Zeiss, Germany) with a 20x objective.

SA-β-gal activity was assessed using a SA-β-gal staining kit (Solarbio, China). Tissue sections or cells were fixed and incubated in SA-β-gal staining solution at 37 °C overnight, protected from light according to the manufacturer's instructions. After staining, slides were washed several times in PBS to stop the reaction and remove excess staining solution. Images were acquired using an optical microscope (Zeiss, Germany) with a 20x objective. To quantify the SA-β-gal positive rate, images were analyzed using ImageJ. A signal intensity threshold was set to identify positive staining, distinguishing it from background. The positive cells were calculated as a percentage of the total cell count in each field of view. For each sample, 4 fields of view were analyzed, and the average positive rate was reported.

Apoptotic cells were detected using a TUNEL staining kit (Servicebio, China). Tissue sections or cells were fixed in 4 % PFA, permeabilized with 0.1 % Triton X-100 in PBS for 10 min, and incubated with TUNEL reaction mixture (containing terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase and fluorescein-labeled dUTP) at 37 °C for 1 h according to the manufacture's instruction. After staining, slides were washed several times in PBS to stop the reaction and mounted. The images were obtained by optical microscope (Zeiss, Germany) with a 20x objective. To quantify the TUNEL positive rate, images were analyzed using ImageJ. A signal intensity threshold was set to identify positive staining, distinguishing it from background. The positive cells were calculated as a percentage of the total cell count in each field of view. For each sample, 4 fields of view were analyzed, and the average positive rate was reported.

Cells were cultured on slides and fixed by 4 % PFA in PBS for 15 min and washed in PBS three times, then permeabilized in 0.1 % Triton-X100 (Sigma) for 15 min at room temperature. Cells were then incubated with anti-PKM2 (1:100) overnight at 4 °C and washed twice in PBS before incubation with secondary immunofluorescent antibody for 1 h at room temperature. Cells were analyzed by microscopy or Elyra 7 Lattice SIM (Zeiss, Jena, Germany) with a 63x objective.

MSC-apoVs were resuspended and blocked with 5 % BSA in PBS for 1 h. Then MSC-apoVs were incubated with anti-PKM2 antibody for 1 h at room temperature. After incubation, the samples were washed with PBS three times, followed by differential centrifugation. MSC-apoVs were incubated in secondary antibody for 1 h at room temperature and subsequently incubated with membrane dye Cellmask Deepred (1:1000) and PE-Annexin V (1:100) for 30 min at 37 °C. MSC-apoVs were analyzed using an Elyra 7 Lattice SIM (Zeiss, Jena, Germany) with a 100x objective.

To assess whether MSC-apoVs carry PKM2 into the nucleus, Z-stack imaging was performed using an Elyra 7 Lattice SIM. MSC-apoVs were isolated from cells of PKM2-eGFP mice, resulting in MSC-apoVs containing PKM2-eGFP. The MSC-apoVs were stained with PKH26 for 5 min at room temperature to label their membranes and then cultured with target cells for 1 h. The cells were stained with Hoechst for 5 min at room temperature to mark the nuclei, fixed, and analyzed by Z-stack imaging. Images were reconstructed in 3D using ZEN software, and 3D reconstruction was generated to confirm nuclear localization.

Circulating EVs were diluted in filtered PBS, dropped onto carbon-coated copper grids and dried at room temperature. The TEM images were captured at 120 kV using the TEM (Tecnai G2 Spirit, FEI, USA).

MSC-apoVs were diluted in filtered PBS to appropriate concentrations and then monitored by ZetaView (Particle Metrix, Germany) for average particle size and electric potential. Experimental data were analyzed using ZetaView analysis software (8.02.31) with a minimum size of 10, a maximum size of 5000, and a minimum brightness of 30.

Circulating extracellular vesicles (EVs) from both Ctrl mice and CP mice were resuspended and blocked with 5 % BSA in PBS for 1 h. Then vesicles were incubated with PE anti-PKM2 antibody (BioLegend, USA) or PE anti-Annexin V (BioLegend, USA) for 1 h at room temperature and washed with PBS three times followed by differential centrifugation. The vesicles were analyzed using a NanoFCM Flow NanoAnalyzer (NanoFCM, China). MSC-apoVs derived from PKM2-eGFP mice were directly analyzed using the same instrument.

Nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins were extracted using a nuclear protein separation kit according to the manufacture's instruction (Solarbio, China). Lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 20 min at 4 °C, and supernatants were collected. Protein concentrations were determined using a BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer's instructions. 20 μg protein was used for electrophoresis and transferred to PVDF membranes (Millipore, Billerica, MA, USA). After transfer, membranes were briefly rinsed with methanol and stained with 0.1 % Ponceau S solution (Sigma-Aldrich, Germany) for 5 min at room temperature to verify protein transfer. Membranes were then washed with distilled water until the background was clear, and images were captured for documentation. Following Ponceau S staining, membranes were blocked for 1 h, incubated with corresponding primary antibody at 4 °C overnight, and then incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h. The primary antibodies are listed in Supplementary Table 1 . Lastly, the membranes were visualized by SuperSignal West Pico Chemiluminescent Substrate (Thermo Fisher, USA) and scanned by a ChemiDoc™ MP imaging system (Bio-Rad, CA, USA).

Statistical and graph analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 9.0 (GraphPad Software, Inc., USA). For two-group comparisons, significance was assessed by unpaired Student's t -test. Differences among multiple groups were analyzed by one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post hoc test. All the data were presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). ns, no significant. ∗ P < 0.05; ∗∗ P < 0.01; ∗∗∗ P < 0.001.
sections.results:
We first investigated whether experimental CP induces persistent systemic inflammation. CP mice were generated by ligation of the bilateral maxillary second molars for different time periods (3 days, 6 days, 15 days, 30 days, or 60 days) ( Fig. S1a ). To mimic clinical periodontitis, we employed a well-established mouse model using porphyromonas gingivalis pre-soaked silk ligature [ 35 ]. In comparison to the control group, mice with ligature-induced periodontitis showed obvious bone resorption after 6 days, and the bone destruction reached its maximum 15 days after induction, with no significant difference seen 30 or 60 days post-induction ( Fig. 1 a and b). We found that the expression levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-17, TNF-α, TNF-β, and IFN-γ in the plasma increased at different stages. IL-6 showed an increasing trend, although it was not statistically significant. Specifically, IL-1β, IL-17, TNF-α, and TNF-β showed a significant rise after 30 and 60 days of ligation but not after 15 days, as determined by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) ( Fig. 1 e). Next, we evaluated the alteration of immunity during CP development by analyzing the ratios of CD4 + , CD8 + , Th17, and Treg cells in cervical lymph node (C-LN), spleen, and peripheral blood ( Fig. 1 c and d). The gating strategy used for flow cytometry analysis was shown in Fig. S1b–e . Flow cytometry analysis showed that the populations of CD4 + , CD8 + , Th17, and Treg cells and the ratio of Th17/Treg as well as CD4 + /CD8 + demonstrated obvious alteration during periodontitis when compared to the control mice. It is well known that CP can develop into systemic inflammation along with disruption of the innate and adaptive immune system [ 7 , [41] , [42] , [43] , [44] ].

Furthermore, we found that mice with short-term periodontitis (15 days) almost completely recovered after the removal of molar ligation followed by a 30-day recovery period ( Fig. 1 f–i). In contrast, mice with long-term periodontitis (60 days) did not recover spontaneously ( Fig. 1 f–i). Therefore, we further examined these two groups to assess differences in histopathological changes and senescent cell accumulation. Our results showed that the 60-day (60d) group had significantly intensified inflammatory responses in the liver, white pulp atrophy in the spleen, decreased capsular space in the kidney, and reduced bone marrow in the femur ( Fig. 1 j). These observations align with findings from previous investigation [ 32 , 45 , 46 ]. Meanwhile, SA-β-Gal staining analysis showed increased accumulation of senescent cells in the liver, spleen, kidney, and femur in the 60d group ( Fig. 1 k and l). Immunofluorescence staining further showed a significant increase in p16, a biomarker of aging, in these tissues in the 60d group ( Fig. 1 m and n). Specifically, after 15 days of ligature-induced periodontitis followed by a 30-day recovery period, no significant histopathological changes were observed in the above organs when compared to controls ( Fig. S1f and S1g ). CBC revealed an increase in white blood cells, and digital photos showed significant splenic enlargement, both indicating systemic inflammation, in the 60d group ( Fig. S1h and S1i ).

We investigated whether 60d CP mice display apoptotic resistance phenotypes in the peripheral blood lymphocytes, spleen, and bone marrow. The levels of pro-apoptotic proteins cleaved caspase 3 and Bax were reduced and the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-xl was increased in the spleen and bone marrow of the CP group when compared to controls, as assessed by Western blotting ( Fig. 2 a and b). Flow cytometry and Western blotting indicated that both periodontitis patients and mice have lower apoptotic rates of peripheral blood lymphocytes than controls ( Fig. 2 c–h). Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) staining showed reduction of apoptosis in the spleen and bone marrow in the CP group ( Fig. 2 i and j). The NFκ-B pathway was active in peripheral blood lymphocyte of CP mice ( Fig. S2a ). Next, we isolated bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMMSCs) from mice. Western blotting revealed activation of the NFκ-B pathway, as indicated by elevated levels of phosphorylated p65 (p-p65) ( Fig. 2 k). Additionally, BMMSCs from CP mice exhibited increased levels of p16, as assessed by Western blotting and IF, along with an increased number of SA-β-Gal + cells ( Fig. 2 k–m, S2b ). The apoptotic rate of BMMSCs was decreased in the CP group ( Fig. 2 n and o). Our findings demonstrate that systemic inflammation triggered by chronic periodontitis induces apoptotic resistance across multiple organs. We treated CP mice with senolytics (dasatinib and quercetin) to determine whether they could inhibit or even reverse local bone loss ( Fig. S3a ). ELISA and CBC results demonstrated that senolytic treatment effectively reduced systemic inflammation ( Fig. 3 e, S3d, S3e ). Additionally, IF and SA-β-Gal staining analysis showed a reduction in the accumulation of senescent cells following senolytic treatment ( Fig. 3 f–i). Importantly, HE and TRAP staining showed significant improvements in local bone defects and a reduction in osteoclast infiltration following the removal of senescent cells ( Fig. 3 a–d). Senolytics rescued apoptosis in the spleen and femur, as shown by TUNEL staining. ( Fig. 3 j and k). Hair whitening was assessed qualitatively as a senescence-associated marker without quantification ( Fig. S3b ); previous studies have validated hair pigmentation changes as reliable indicators of aging and senescence in mice [ 47 , 48 ]. Body weight was measured at the study endpoint to assess general health following senolytic treatment, serving as an indirect indicator of efficacy [ 48 ]. Although longitudinal tracking would provide more detailed insight, endpoint measurements still offer valuable information ( Fig. S3c ). These findings suggest that the prolonged presence of local chronic inflammation leads to the systemic accumulation of senescent cells, which in turn contributes to the pathological process of local inflammation. Systemic treatment aimed at removing senescent cells could offer a promising therapeutic strategy for mitigating CP which cannot be reversed by the current standard of care. Since apoptotic cells secrete vesicles of various sizes, we collected human plasma extracellular vesicles (EVs) from both16,000 g and 120,000 g centrifugation to assess the systemic effects on CP ( Fig. S4a ). We performed DIA-based proteomic profiling to investigate differences in EV characteristics between periodontitis patients (CP) and healthy controls (Ctrl). Partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) showed a clear separation between the CP and Ctrl groups ( Fig. 4 a). The CP group displayed a tight clustering, indicating a relatively homogeneous profile, whereas the Ctrl group exhibited a broader distribution, potentially reflecting higher biological heterogeneity among healthy individuals. The heatmap ( Fig. 4 b) and volcano plot ( Fig. 4 c) revealed that numerous proteins were downregulated in EVs derived from CP patients compared to the controls. This suggests disease-specific alterations in EV profiles, likely associated with periodontitis pathogenesis. Functional enrichment analysis using Gene Ontology Biological Processes (GOBP) and KEGG pathways highlighted key differences in EV protein functions. Proteins upregulated in CP EVs were enriched in immune response-related processes (such as “immune effector process” and “complement activation”), while downregulated proteins were primarily involved in “metabolic processes” and “cell death” ( Fig. 4 d and e). Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) further supported these findings, confirming that gene sets associated with immune response were upregulated in CP EVs ( Fig. 4 f). Conversely, metabolic processes and apoptotic pathways were significantly downregulated ( Fig. 4 g and h). Key proteins contributing to these enriched pathways were identified ( Fig. 4 i and j, S4b ). Notably, pyruvate kinase M (PKM), a critical regulator of metabolic processes, was significantly decreased in EVs from CP patients, alongside other proteins implicated in EV function and immune regulation. Given that CP can lead to systemic pathological changes, we hypothesized that a systemic treatment approach could alleviate both local and systemic disease phenotypes associated with CP. Previous studies have demonstrated that MSCs possess strong immune regulation abilities and exhibit significant anti-aging effects [ 51 ]. Many studies have shown that a large proportion of transplanted MSCs ultimately undergo apoptosis, but this does not compromise their therapeutic value and may indeed be key to success, as it leads to the production of numerous MSC-apoVs that exert various beneficial effects [ 52 , 53 ]. Therefore, we administered adipose-derived MSC-apoVs and adipose-derived MSCs intravenously to treat the CP mice. The isolation process and morphology of MSC-apoVs are shown in Fig. S6a–c , while the intervention timeline and treatment grouping are illustrated in Fig. S6d . Both MSC-apoVs and MSCs promoted local bone regeneration, as assessed by HE staining and TRAP staining ( Fig. 6 a–d). Additionally, flow cytometry and HE staining demonstrated that this strategy inhibited systemic inflammation and improved pathological changes in the liver, spleen, kidney, and bone marrow ( Fig. 6 e, S6f-h ). SA-β-Gal and p16 IF staining indicated that MSC-apoVs and MSCs reduced senescent cell accumulation in these tissues ( Fig. 6 f–i). Furthermore, they alleviated apoptotic resistance of the bone marrow, as assessed by Western blotting ( Fig. S6e ). The apoptotic rate was also significantly improved in spleen and femur following MSC-apoV or MSC treatment ( Fig. 6 j and k). These data suggest that both MSC-apoVs and MSCs can effectively alleviate local and systemic symptoms in CP mice. To confirm the contribution of PKM2 carried by MSC-apoVs in systemic therapy, we evaluated the dose-dependent therapeutic effects of PKM2 in CP mice. Specifically, we used MSC-apoVs derived from PKM2 +/− mice, which have reduced PKM2 (PKM2 low MSC-apoVs), to treat mice with long-term CP and compared them with MSC-apoVs from WT mice containing normal levels of PKM2 (PKM2 + MSC-apoVs) ( Fig. S7a–d ). Interestingly, we found that the systemic administration of PKM2 + MSC-apoVs, but not PKM2 low MSC-apoVs, markedly mitigated local alveolar bone loss ( Fig. 7 a and b), decreased the number of jaw osteoclasts ( Fig. 7 c and d), and suppressed systemic inflammation in CP mice ( Fig. 7 e–g, S7e , S7f, S7g). SA-β-Gal staining and p16 IF analysis further indicated that PKM2 is crucial for MSC-apoVs in alleviating senescence in the liver, kidney, and bone marrow ( Fig. 7 h–k). Additionally, the apoptotic rates in the spleen and femur were significantly increased only in the PKM2 + MSC-apoVs group ( Fig. 7 l and m). PKM2 + MSC-apoV treatment also promoted the expression of Fas, cleaved caspase-3, and Bax, while reducing the expression of Bcl-xl in the spleen and bone marrow, thereby improving apoptotic resistance ( Fig. S7h and S7i ). We concluded on this basis that PKM2 plays a pivotal role in mediating the therapeutic effects of MSC-apoVs in CP mice, highlighting the therapeutic potential of PKM2 + MSC-apoVs in managing senescence and inflammation. Furthermore, these findings suggest that PKM2 + MSC-apoVs hold promise as a treatment for age-related inflammatory diseases. Next, we observed that the PKM2 level was increased in the cytoplasm and decreased in the nucleus in CP BMMSCs, but this imbalance could be rescued by PKM2 + MSC-apoV treatment ( Fig. 8 f and g). PKM2 IF staining revealed the formation of PKM2 condensates in the cytoplasm in the CP group, which was significantly reduced after treatment with PKM2 + MSC-apoVs. However, this effect was not observed with PKM2 kd MSC-apoVs ( Fig. 8 h).

To analyze the impact of long-term low-grade inflammation on apoptosis, we treated BMMSCs in vitro with a low dose of an inflammatory cytokine, specifically TNF-α or IL-17. Western blotting and flow cytometry analysis showed that treatment with TNF-α or IL-17 for 9 days directly inhibited the apoptosis of BMMSCs ( Fig. S8e–g ), accompanied by an accumulation of senescent cells, as shown by SA-β-Gal staining ( Fig. S8h and S8i ). Furthermore, Western blot analysis was performed to detect phosphorylated NF-κB protein levels. Treatment with TNF-α or IL-17 resulted in increased p-p65 expression ( Fig. S8e ). Moreover, this treatment led to elevated cytoplasmic PKM2 and p16 levels and reduced nuclear PKM2 levels in BMMSCs ( Fig. S8j ). PKM2 + MSC-apoVs were able to restore the PKM2 protein level in the nucleus, but they had no significant effect on PKM2 levels in the cytoplasm ( Fig. 8 i).

PKM2 IF staining showed that MSC-apoVs facilitated the transport of PKM2 into the nucleus ( Fig. 8 j).

To further validate the nuclear localization of MSC-apoVs and PKM2, we performed Z-stack imaging using Elyra 7 Lattice SIM. The reconstructed three-dimensional images confirmed that both MSC-apoVs and PKM2 signals colocalized with DAPI staining within the nucleus in a subset of cells ( Fig. 8 k). In addition to observe the effect of directly delivering PKM2 into the nucleus via apoVs, we investigated whether apoVs could also influence the phosphorylation status of endogenous PKM2 in recipient MSCs, thereby promoting its nuclear translocation through post-translational modification. Specifically, we examined phosphorylation at two key regulatory sites Ser37 and Tyr105, which are known to distinctly regulate PKM2's subcellular localization and functional state [ 54 , 55 ]. Western blot analysis demonstrated that treatment with PKM2 + MSC-apoVs selectively enhanced phosphorylation at the Ser37 site, whereas phosphorylation at Tyr105 remained unchanged ( Fig. 8 l and S8k ). These results suggest that MSC-apoVs not only serve as direct carriers of nuclear-targeted PKM2, but also modulate intracellular signaling to promote the nuclear import of endogenous PKM2 through Ser37 phosphorylation. These data reveal that PKM2 + MSC-apoVs reverse senescence and improve apoptotic resistance by restoring the nuclear localization of PKM2, which is disrupted by chronic inflammation.
sections.discussion:
Epidemiological studies indicate that chronic inflammation is related to apoptotic resistance. The accumulation of senescent cells in diseased regions is a common occurrence in localized inflammatory conditions, including periodontitis, arthritis, and pneumonia [ [56] , [57] , [58] , [59] ]. In addition, inflammation can inhibit the apoptosis of immune cells. For instance, colitis can be exacerbated by promoting T cell apoptotic resistance in the intestinal mucosa [ 60 ]. In patients with autoimmune diseases like systemic lupus erythematosus, T cells exhibit apoptotic resistance and contribute to the inflammatory process [ 61 ]. Previous studies have demonstrated that pro-inflammatory factors, including IL-17, TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, can directly induce cells to become resistant to apoptosis [ [62] , [63] , [64] , [65] ]. However, whether the systemic inflammation triggered by periodontitis can induce apoptotic resistance and exert systemic effects remains unknown. In our study, we found that prolonged local inflammation can induce accumulation of senescent cells and apoptotic resistance in multiple organs of CP mice. This systemic accumulation of senescent cells may be one of the key factors contributing to the limited treatment efficacy of localized chronic inflammatory diseases.

Although CP mice used in this study may not fully replicate the complexity of human periodontal disease, a few of inflammatory pathways involved in human periodontitis, such as elevated levels of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-17, are observed in CP mice [ 4 , 66 , 67 ]. Furthermore, apoptotic resistance under chronic inflammatory stress has been documented in both human and murine immune cells, supporting the translational relevance of this model. These shared mechanisms strengthen the rationale for using CP mice to investigate the systemic impact of periodontitis, particularly in relation to senescence and apoptotic dysregulation. Nonetheless, we acknowledge the limitations of this approach and emphasize the need for future validation in human samples or more clinically representative models to fully establish the translational significance of our findings.

Senolytics are a class of therapeutic agents designed to selectively eliminate senescent cells with secreting a range of pro-inflammatory and tissue-degrading factors collectively known as the SASP [ 68 ]. The accumulation of senescent cells has been implicated in various chronic inflammatory diseases, including CP, where they sustain local inflammation and impair tissue homeostasis. While small-molecule senolytics dominate current strategies for eliminating senescent cells, recent studies show that extracellular vesicle-based delivery systems can enhance specificity and bioavailability [ 69 ]. Although such research remains limited, preliminary evidence supports their promise as a novel senolytic platform. Our study contributes to this emerging field by demonstrating the therapeutic potential of MSC-apoVs in modulating systemic senescence and inflammation.

Recent studies have highlighted a causal role of cellular senescence in the pathogenesis of CP. Chu et al. demonstrated that targeted elimination of senescent cells in gingival tissues significantly attenuated disease severity in CP mice [ 57 , 70 , 71 ]. These findings underscore the pathological contribution of senescent cells to CP. While their work focused on localized gingival senescence, our study expands this understanding by demonstrating that CP leads to a systemic accumulation of senescent cells across multiple organs. This systemic senescence may drive persistent inflammation and tissue dysfunction beyond the oral cavity, suggesting a broader role for senescence in CP-induced systemic pathological phenotypes.

In line with these findings, our study supports the therapeutic potential of senolytics in CP. Previous work has shown that dasatinib and quercetin (D + Q) can alleviate age-related periodontal tissue damage by reducing local senescence and inflammation [ 72 ]. In our study, D + Q treatment significantly reduced systemic senescent cell burden and alleviated bone loss that could not be reversed by removing local stimuli alone. Notably, these senescent cells were local inflammation-induced rather than age-related. We highlight the potential of systemic therapeutic strategies to address persistent local inflammation, thereby contributing to the management of CP and other refractory chronic inflammatory conditions.

Apoptosis plays a vital role in preserving the homeostasis of organs and tissues [ 73 ]. Far from being discarded as waste, apoptotic metabolite-rich apoVs actually carry multiple materials and signaling molecules that participate in cell communication, immune regulation, and tissue repair [ 74 ]. It is increasingly recognized that chronic inflammation leads to the local accumulation of apoptosis-resistant cells. Previous research has primarily concentrated on the role of chronic inflammation in fostering apoptotic resistance, recognizing that cells resistant to apoptosis can exacerbate inflammation [ 75 ]. However, less attention has been given to how dysregulated apoptosis leads to reduced apoV production, which may further exacerbate inflammation and impair tissue homeostasis. The findings presented in this study underscore that chronic inflammation directly triggers apoptotic resistance, resulting in a reduction of circulating EVs, which contributes to CP-induced systemic effects. The proteomic analysis of these EVs revealed alterations in the key regulatory protein PKM2 under the conditions of apoptotic resistance caused by chronic inflammation.

In the human body, 50–70 billion cells undergo apoptosis daily, releasing abundant apoVs during this process [ 17 ]. They can serve as regulators for multiple physiological and pathological processes [ 76 ]. However, in the condition of apoptotic resistance, reduction of apoVs may play a vital role in the process of inflammation. ApoVs are a specific type of EVs with a lipid bilayer surface structure, loaded with a variety of cargos. Our previous study showed that systemic administration of MSC-apoVs can restore tissue homeostasis, thereby promoting bone regeneration and regulating the inflammatory response. For instance, they can improve osteopenia by transferring multiple cellular factors, inhibit the activation of T cells in SLE and arthritis, and combat type 2 diabetes by restoring the homeostasis of liver macrophages [ 16 , 17 , 20 , 77 ].

ApoVs are larger extracellular particles released by cells during apoptosis, typically ranging from 100 to 1000 nm in size, which is significantly larger than exosomes (30–150 nm in diameter) [ 78 ]. Under induction conditions, apoVs are produced at higher yields, facilitating their large-scale preparation and providing advantages in production efficiency. Due to their larger size, apoVs are easier to distinguish and isolate during separation and purification compared to exosomes. Our previous research found that MSC-apoVs express specific markers, including Fas, calnexin, and calreticulin, distinguishing them from exosomes [ 40 ]. In this study, we discovered that PKM2 can also serve to distinguish MSC-apoVs from exosomes. Additionally, the high proportion of PKM2 + MSC-apoVs within the total apoV population further simplifies purification and reduces associated costs. Our previous studies demonstrated that freeze-dried MSC-apoVs retain robust biological activity after being stored at room temperature for one month, supporting their potential for future clinical translation and industrial-scale production. We identified that MSC-apoVs inherit PKM2 from their parent cells, and this protein is critical to their therapeutic effects in CP mice and found that PKM2 + MSC-apoVs exhibit potential senolytic properties. These findings suggest that PKM2 + MSC-apoVs may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for mitigating inflammation-driven senescence and tissue degeneration.

PKM2, a key glycolytic enzyme, has emerged as a multifaceted regulator beyond its canonical metabolic role [ 79 ]. PKM2 is a pivotal player in orchestrating inflammatory responses. It actively participates in the regulation of the balance between pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory states, and exacerbates the inflammatory process in pathological states [ 22 , 80 ]. PKM2 can be induced by the NF-κB pathway and further enhances NF-κB signaling [ 81 ]. It has also been shown to exert dual roles in regulating apoptosis as both a promoter and suppressor of programmed cell death [ 50 ]. The NF-κB pathway in which PKM2 participates plays a crucial role in the regulation of inflammation and apoptosis of cells. Activation of NF-κB can lead to the production of various pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6) and upregulate the expression of anti-apoptotic proteins which inhibit the activation of caspases, the key executors of apoptosis [ 82 ]. Here we showed that low-grade inflammation activated the NF-κB pathway, leading to PKM2 condensates in the cytoplasm and preventing PKM2 from entering the nucleus, ultimately resulting in resistance to apoptosis. We further revealed that PKM2 carried by MSC-apoVs is transported to the nucleus to facilitate cell apoptosis.

Moreover, our findings reveal that MSC-apoVs not only directly deliver PKM2 into the nucleus but also promote ERK-dependent phosphorylation of endogenous PKM2 at Ser37, thereby facilitating its nuclear translocation. This nuclear localization of PKM2 is critical for inducing apoptosis in senescent cells, contributing to the clearance of damaged or aged cells under chronic inflammatory stress. Importantly, phosphorylation at Tyr105, which regulates PKM2's metabolic activity and oligomerization, remains unchanged, indicating that MSC-apoVs specifically enhance PKM2 nuclear import without affecting its metabolic functions. Together, these results highlight a novel mechanism by which MSC-apoVs modulate intracellular signaling to promote senescent cell apoptosis via PKM2 nuclear translocation, offering potential therapeutic insights for inflammation-associated aging.
sections.conclusion: In conclusion, this study elucidates the critical role of apoptotic resistance in the pathogenesis of CP and highlights the systemic consequences of local inflammation-induced senescence. We demonstrate that CP drives the accumulation of apoptosis-resistant senescent cells across multiple organs, contributing to sustained inflammation and tissue degeneration. Mechanistically, we identify PKM2 as a key regulatory molecule whose nuclear exclusion under inflammatory stress mediates apoptosis resistance. Importantly, we show that MSC-apoVs enriched with PKM2 restore apoptotic sensitivity by directly delivering PKM2 into the nucleus and enhance ERK-mediated Ser37 phosphorylation of endogenous PKM2 to promote its nuclear translocation. Systemic administration of PKM2 + MSC-apoVs reduced senescent cell burden, ameliorated bone loss, diminished osteoclast infiltration, normalized apoptosis in lymphoid tissues, and attenuated systemic inflammation. These findings reveal a novel therapeutic strategy for targeting inflammation-driven senescence using MSC-apoVs. Beyond CP, this approach may offer broad applicability in treating other chronic inflammatory diseases marked by apoptotic dysregulation. Further research is warranted to optimize delivery strategies and evaluate long-term efficacy in clinical settings.
